name: Local Models for Patient Data
title: Local Models for Patient Data
answer: Local models for patient data are machine learning systems that process protected health information on hardware controlled by a healthcare organization, rather than sending it to a third-party cloud. This scope covers models deployed inside hospital networks, on clinic workstations, or on edge devices such as ultrasound carts and bedside monitors. The focus is on keeping patient records, images, and waveforms within the institution's security perimeter while still using AI for diagnosis support, documentation, and triage. Local deployment is often chosen when data residency rules, latency requirements, or network reliability make cloud inference impractical. The topic also includes models that are trained or fine-tuned on local patient data without that data leaving the organization.

This scope covers models deployed inside hospital networks, on clinic workstations, or on edge devices such as ultrasound carts and bedside monitors. The focus is on keeping patient records, images, and waveforms within the institution's security perimeter while still using AI for diagnosis support, documentation, and triage. The topic also includes models that are trained or fine-tuned on local patient data without that data leaving the organization.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Local models run on servers, workstations, or dedicated appliances that the healthcare organization owns or leases. Common hardware includes GPU-equipped servers for inference and fine-tuning, CPU-only servers for smaller models, and edge devices with embedded accelerators for point-of-care use. The infrastructure must meet the organization's existing requirements for physical security, backup, and disaster recovery. Many local deployments use containerized model serving platforms that run on the hospital's virtual machine or Kubernetes environment. Network isolation, encrypted storage, and access controls are part of the base infrastructure rather than optional add-ons.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by first selecting a model that is licensed for local use and has acceptable performance on the organization's own patient population. The model is then installed on local hardware, often inside a container or virtual machine, and connected to the electronic health record or imaging archive through controlled interfaces. Inference runs on local data without transmitting patient identifiers to the model vendor, though logs and performance metrics may be shared in de-identified form. Fine-tuning or retraining on local data is done with the same governance controls as any other clinical data processing, including approval from data protection and clinical safety officers. Validation on local data is a standard step before clinical use, because patient demographics and equipment can shift model behavior.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance center on who can access the model, the data, and the outputs, and on what happens when the model is wrong. Local deployment reduces the risk of a third party seeing patient data, but it does not remove the need for access logs, audit trails, and role-based permissions. The organization remains responsible for model performance, patient harm, and compliance with health privacy law, even if the model was built by an outside vendor. Provenance requires recording which model version, training data, and fine-tuning steps were used for each patient encounter, so that a later review can reconstruct the decision. Product liability and wrongful death claims against AI companies are tracked on this site, and local deployment can shift some but not all of that liability to the healthcare provider.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Local models are moving toward smaller, more efficient architectures that can run on modest hospital hardware without a dedicated GPU cluster. Federated learning and split learning are being explored as ways to improve a shared model using local patient data without centralizing that data. Regulatory guidance is likely to treat local AI as a medical device function of the hospital's own IT system, with clearer expectations for change control and post-market surveillance. The site's compliance and regulation pages will continue to track how local deployment affects device classification and data protection duties. Over time, local models may become the default for high-risk patient data, with cloud used only for non-sensitive tasks or for models that cannot run locally.
